6.G-1#1.title: Tile a bathroom floor
6.G-1#1.text: Think of a floor that is 7 feet by 3 feet, covered with tiles that are 1 foot on each side. You could count the tiles by columns: there are 7 columns with 3 tiles in each, and 3 counted seven times is 21. Counting by rows gives 21 as well. The number of tiles is the area, and it is the same whichever way you count.

6.G-1#2.title: Cut a sheet of paper
6.G-1#2.text: Take a sheet of paper 6 units wide and 4 units tall. Its area is 6 × 4 = 24. Cut it from one corner to the opposite corner. You get two triangles that match exactly when you stack them, so each one has area 12. That is the same as ½ × 6 × 4. A triangle that leans can be split into two of these corner-cut triangles, so the half rule still holds.

6.G-1#3.title: The leaning ladder
6.G-1#3.text: A ladder 10 feet long leans against a wall and touches it 8 feet above the ground. How high does it reach? Only 8 feet, not 10. The 10 is the slanted side, and the 8 is the height. Your own height is measured the same way: standing straight against the wall, not leaning. Use the straight-up number in the area formula.

6.G-1#4.title: Split 7 into 5 + 2
6.G-1#4.text:
Cut the rectangle into two smaller ones with a line: a 5-by-3 piece and a 2-by-3 piece.
The first holds 5 × 3 = 15 squares and the second holds 2 × 3 = 6 squares.
Together that is 15 + 6 = 21 square units, the same as 7 × 3.

6.G-1#5.title: Box it, then halve
6.G-1#5.text: Draw a rectangle around the triangle that is 8 wide and 5 tall. It covers 8 × 5 = 40 square units. The triangle fills exactly half of that rectangle, so its area is 40 ÷ 2 = 20 square units. This multiplies first and halves last, and it lands on the same 20.

6.G-1#6.title: Halve the height instead
6.G-1#6.text: The half can go on either number. Half of the height 4 is 2. Picture the top of the triangle cut off and tucked in beside the bottom part, making a rectangle 10 wide and 2 tall. Its area is 10 × 2 = 20 square units. Halving the base works too: 5 × 4 = 20.

6.G-1#7.title: Use 6 × 10, then trim
6.G-1#7.text: Nine is one less than ten, so start with an easier rectangle. A 6-by-10 rectangle has area 60. The 6-by-9 rectangle is one strip of 6 squares narrower, so take that strip away: 60 − 6 = 54 square units. No half is needed because a rectangle is the whole box.

6.G-1#8.title: Two copies make a parallelogram
6.G-1#8.text: Make a second copy of the triangle, flip it, and fit it against the first. The pair forms a parallelogram with base 12 and height 5, so its area is 12 × 5 = 60. One triangle is half of the pair: 60 ÷ 2 = 30 square units.

6.G-1#9.title: Multiply first, halve last
6.G-1#9.text: When you are not sure which number to halve, leave the half until the end. Multiply the base and height: 7 × 6 = 42. That is the rectangle around the triangle. Now take half of it: 42 ÷ 2 = 21 square units. An even product is easy to halve, so this order always works when one number is even.

6.G-1#10.title: Split into two right triangles
6.G-1#10.text: Draw the height. Suppose it lands 2 units from one end of the base, so the base splits into 2 and 4. The left piece is half of a 2-by-4 box: 8 ÷ 2 = 4. The right piece is half of a 4-by-4 box: 16 ÷ 2 = 8. Together 4 + 8 = 12 square units. Wherever the height lands, the two pieces add to 12.

6.G-2#1.title: Like a dot-to-dot puzzle
6.G-2#1.text: In a dot-to-dot puzzle you join dot 1 to dot 2 to dot 3, and the picture appears. Vertices work the same way. Joining (1, 1), (5, 1), (5, 4), (1, 4) in that order and back to the start draws a rectangle. Join them as (1, 1), (5, 4), (5, 1), (1, 4) and the lines cross like a bow tie. Same dots, wrong order, wrong shape.

6.G-2#2.title: Ride the elevator
6.G-2#2.text: Think of x as the street a building stands on and y as the floor. Going from (2, 1) to (2, 6) means staying in the building on street 2 and riding from floor 1 to floor 6. The elevator passes floors 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6, so it climbs 5 floors. The street number never changes, so it plays no part in the distance.

6.G-2#3.title: Houses on one street
6.G-2#3.text: Two houses stand on the same street, at number 1 and number 7. The street is the shared y-value, 3. Walking from house 1 you pass 2, 3, 4, 5, 6 and arrive at 7, which is 6 steps. You never cross to another street, so only the house numbers matter. That is the points (1, 3) and (7, 3): 6 units apart.

6.G-2#4.title: Move the shape, same answer
6.G-2#4.text: A rectangle has corners (2, 3), (7, 3), (7, 6) and (2, 6). Its sides are 7 − 2 = 5 and 6 − 3 = 3, so the area is 15 and the perimeter is 16. Now slide it so one corner sits at (0, 0). The corners become (0, 0), (5, 0), (5, 3), (0, 3). The sides are still 5 and 3, so nothing changes. Only the lengths matter.

6.G-2#5.title: Count the jumps up
6.G-2#5.text: Put a finger on (2, 1) and hop up one grid line at a time. The hops land on y = 2, 3, 4, 5 and 6. That is 5 hops, so the side is 5 units long. You can check with addition: starting at 1 and adding 5 gives 6, the y-value of the top point.

6.G-2#6.title: Add on to check
6.G-2#6.text: Ask what must be added to the smaller x-value to reach the larger one. Starting at x = 1, add 6 and you arrive at x = 7. So the two corners are 6 units apart. Counting grid lines agrees: 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7 is six steps to the right along the line y = 3.

6.G-2#7.title: Count the unit squares
6.G-2#7.text: Draw the rectangle on grid paper. Between y = 0 and y = 3 there are 3 rows of squares. Each row runs from x = 0 to x = 4, so it holds 4 squares. Counting by rows gives 4 + 4 + 4 = 12 square units. No subtraction is needed when the grid is in front of you.

6.G-2#8.title: Slide both points up 2
6.G-2#8.text: Sliding a segment does not change its length. Move both points up 2 units so the lower one sits on the x-axis. The point (3, −2) becomes (3, 0) and the point (3, 5) becomes (3, 7). Now the distance is easy to read: from 0 up to 7 is 7 units.

6.G-2#9.title: Build the square and count
6.G-2#9.text: A side of 5 means the other two corners are (5, 5) and (0, 5). Draw the square on the grid. It has 5 rows, and every row has 5 unit squares. Count by fives: 5, 10, 15, 20, 25. The area is 25 square units, the same as 5 × 5.

6.G-2#10.title: Walk around the corners
6.G-2#10.text: Start at (0, 0) and walk the border. To (6, 0) is 6 units. Up to (6, 3) is 3 units. Back to (0, 3) is 6 units. Down to (0, 0) is 3 units. Keep a running total as you go: 6, then 9, then 15, then 18. The trip around is 18 units.

6.G-2#11.title: Straighten out the border
6.G-2#11.text: Imagine the border is a piece of string. Cut it at one corner and pull it straight. It is made of four pieces: 6, 3, 6 and 3. Slide the equal pieces next to each other: 6 + 6 = 12 and 3 + 3 = 6. The whole string is 12 + 6 = 18 units long, which is the perimeter.

6.G-3#1.title: Slice the box a different way
6.G-3#1.text: Take the same 2 × 3 × 5 box and look at it from the side. One side wall is 3 by 5, so a slice against it holds 15 cubes. The box is 2 slices thick, so it holds 15 + 15 = 30 cubes. Starting from the floor gave 6 × 5 = 30. Whichever face you start from, you count the same cubes, so the three numbers can be multiplied in any order.

6.G-3#2.title: The fish tank test
6.G-3#2.text: A fish tank has a bottom that is 4 by 3. Multiply those two numbers and you get 12 square units. That tells you how much glass covers the bottom, but not how much water goes in. For water you also need the depth. If the tank is 2 deep, the water takes 12 × 2 = 24 cubic units. Two numbers describe the glass. Three numbers describe the water.

6.G-3#3.title: Stack two half boxes
6.G-3#3.text: A box is 4 by 6 and only ½ unit tall. Put a second box just like it on top. Together they make a box 4 by 6 by 1, which holds 24 unit cubes. The two boxes are equal, so each holds 24 ÷ 2 = 12 cubic units. The formula agrees: 4 × 6 × ½ = 12. A fraction edge just means part of a full layer.

6.G-3#4.title: Start from a side wall
6.G-3#4.text: Look at the 3-by-5 face instead of the floor. A slice one cube thick against that face holds 3 × 5 = 15 cubes. The box is 2 cubes thick in the other direction, so there are 2 slices. That gives 15 × 2 = 30 cubic units, the same total as floor times layers.

6.G-3#5.title: Add three layers of nine
6.G-3#5.text: The bottom layer of the cube is a 3-by-3 square, which is 9 unit cubes. The cube is 3 tall, so there are three layers exactly alike. Add them one at a time: 9 + 9 = 18, and 18 + 9 = 27. The cube holds 27 cubic units.

6.G-3#6.title: Slices from the end
6.G-3#6.text: Look at the box from its end, where the face is 2 by 3. That face shows 6 cubes. The box is 4 long, so it is like a loaf cut into 4 slices of 6 cubes each. Count by sixes: 6, 12, 18, 24. The volume is 24 cubic units.

6.G-3#7.title: Pair the half with the 4
6.G-3#7.text: Multiplying can be done in any order, so let the fraction meet an even number first. Half of 4 is 2. Now the box is like one with edges 2 and 3, and 2 × 3 = 6 cubic units. Pairing ½ with an even edge removes the fraction in one step.

6.G-3#8.title: Halve the 6 first
6.G-3#8.text: Let the half act on one edge before any other multiplying. Half of 6 is 3. What is left is 3 × 4 = 12 cubic units. You could also halve the 4 to get 2, and then 2 × 6 = 12. Every order gives 12, so pick the one that feels easiest.

6.G-3#9.title: Stack layers until 40
6.G-3#9.text: The floor is 4 by 2, so each layer one unit tall holds 8 cubes. Keep adding layers and count by eights: 8, 16, 24, 32, 40. The count reaches the volume of 40 on the fifth layer. So the box is 5 units tall, with no division needed.

6.G-3#10.title: Slices instead of layers
6.G-3#10.text: Turn the box and cut it the other way. The end face is 4 by 3, which shows 12 cubes. The box is 5 long, so there are 5 slices of 12. Counting by twelves gives 12, 24, 36, 48, 60. The volume is 60 cubic units, the same as three layers of 20.

6.G-4#1.title: Unfold a small gift box
6.G-4#1.text: Picture a gift box that is 3 long, 2 wide and 1 tall. Unfold it and you find six flat pieces: two that are 3 by 2 (the lid and the base), two that are 3 by 1 (the long sides) and two that are 2 by 1 (the short ends). Nothing new was made and nothing was lost. The net is just the same six faces lying side by side.

6.G-4#2.title: Stickers on a block
6.G-4#2.text: Cover a 2 × 2 × 2 block with square stickers that are 1 unit on each side, with no gaps and no overlaps. Each face needs 4 stickers. There are 6 faces, so you use 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 + 4 = 24 stickers. That count is the surface area: 24 square units. Stickers are flat squares, which is why the unit is square, not cubic.

6.G-4#3.title: Look around a room
6.G-4#3.text: A room is a box you can stand in. The floor and the ceiling are the same size. The two long walls match each other, and so do the two short walls. For a room 5 long, 4 wide and 3 tall, the floor is 20, a long wall is 15 and a short wall is 12. One of each adds to 47, and doubling gives 94 square units for all six.

6.G-4#4.title: Trace the footprint
6.G-4#4.text: Set the box down on its 2-by-3 face on grid paper and trace around it. The outline covers 2 rows of 3 squares. Counting them gives 3 + 3 = 6 squares. So that face has an area of 6 square units. The height of 1 does not matter for this face.

6.G-4#5.title: A band plus two ends
6.G-4#5.text: The four side faces join into one strip that wraps around the cube. The strip is 2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 8 long and 2 tall, so its area is 16. The top and the bottom are 4 each, which adds 8. Altogether the surface is 16 + 8 = 24 square units.

6.G-4#6.title: Three pairs of faces
6.G-4#6.text: Group the six faces in opposite pairs. The top and bottom are 9 each, so that pair is 18. The front and back also make 18, and so do the left and right. Add the pairs: 18 + 18 + 18 = 54 square units.

6.G-4#7.title: Count it like quarters
6.G-4#7.text: Each face has area 25, the same as the cents in a quarter. Four quarters make 100 cents, and two more make 50 cents. Six quarters are worth 150 cents. In the same way, six faces of 25 cover 150 square units.

6.G-4#8.title: Wrap a label around
6.G-4#8.text: Sit the box on its 2-by-3 face. A label around the four sides is as long as the trip around that face: 2 + 3 + 2 + 3 = 10. The box is 1 tall, so the label covers 10 × 1 = 10. The top and bottom are 6 each, adding 12. The total is 10 + 12 = 22 square units.

6.G-4#9.title: Fold the net in your head
6.G-4#9.text: Many box nets look like a cross: a row of 4 rectangles with 1 flap above and 1 flap below. Fold it in your mind. The row of 4 wraps around to become the front, right, back and left. The two flaps close the top and the bottom. That is 4 + 1 + 1 = 6 faces, so a net with fewer than 6 pieces is missing one.

6.G-4#10.title: Band around, plus two ends
6.G-4#10.text: Stand the box on its 3-by-4 face, so it is 5 tall. A band around the four sides is 3 + 4 + 3 + 4 = 14 long and 5 tall, which covers 14 × 5 = 70. The top and the bottom are 12 each, adding 24. The surface area is 70 + 24 = 94 square units.

6.G-5#1.title: One L-shape, two cuts
6.G-5#1.text: An L-shape is 6 wide along the bottom and 5 tall on the left. Its tall part is 2 wide and its low part is 2 tall. Cut it with an up-and-down line: a 2-by-5 tower and a 4-by-2 block, 10 + 8 = 18. Cut it with a side-to-side line instead: a 6-by-2 strip and a 2-by-3 block, 12 + 6 = 18. Both cuts give 18.

6.G-5#2.title: Tiles for two rooms
6.G-5#2.text: A kitchen floor takes 12 tiles and the hallway next to it takes 6 tiles. The doorway between them is only a line, so no tile belongs to both rooms and no part of the floor is left bare. To tile both you buy 12 + 6 = 18 tiles. Adding the areas of the pieces of a shape works for the same reason.

6.G-5#3.title: A picture frame
6.G-5#3.text: A wooden frame measures 10 by 8 on the outside, and the opening for the photo is 8 by 6. How much wood shows? The full outline covers 10 × 8 = 80 square units, but the opening has no wood in it. The opening is 8 × 6 = 48. The wood covers 80 − 48 = 32 square units. Subtracting is quicker than adding four separate strips.

6.G-5#4.title: Subtract from the surrounding box
6.G-5#4.text: Draw one big rectangle around the whole L. It is 9 wide and 2 + 2 = 4 tall, so it covers 36. The top strip is only 4 wide, so a gap 9 − 4 = 5 wide and 2 tall is empty. The gap is 5 × 2 = 10. The L covers 36 − 10 = 26 square units.

6.G-5#5.title: Skip-count the columns
6.G-5#5.text: Stand the joined shape so its columns are 4 squares tall. The first rectangle has 3 columns: count 4, 8, 12. The second rectangle adds 2 more columns, so keep counting: 16, 20. Every square has been counted once, and the combined area is 20 square units.

6.G-5#6.title: Split what is left
6.G-5#6.text: Picture the hole at a corner. A full strip 5 wide and 5 − 2 = 3 tall sits beside it, with area 15. Next to the hole there is a piece 5 − 2 = 3 wide and 2 tall, with area 6. The part that remains is 15 + 6 = 21 square units. Moving the hole somewhere else would not change the amount left.

6.G-5#7.title: Flatten the roof
6.G-5#7.text: A triangle with base 6 and height 2 covers the same area as a rectangle 6 wide and 1 tall, because half of the height is 1. Trade the roof for that flat strip. Now the house is one rectangle 6 wide and 3 + 1 = 4 tall. Its area is 6 × 4 = 24 square units.

6.G-5#8.title: Think in quarters
6.G-5#8.text: Fold the 10-by-10 square in half both ways. It splits into four 5-by-5 squares, and each one covers 25. The corner bite removes exactly one of the four. Three are left, so the area is 3 × 25 = 75 square units.

6.G-5#9.title: Whole box minus the notch
6.G-5#9.text: Skip the hunt for missing sides and use the outside measurements. A full rectangle 8 wide and 5 tall covers 40. The notch is 3 wide and 2 tall, so it takes away 6. The L covers 40 − 6 = 34 square units, which matches the answer from splitting.

6.G-5#10.title: Split the L instead
6.G-5#10.text: Take the bite to be 2 wide and 4 tall. Draw a line level with the bottom of the bite. Below it is a full strip 8 wide and 6 − 4 = 2 tall, with area 16. Above it is a piece 8 − 2 = 6 wide and 4 tall, with area 24. Together they cover 16 + 24 = 40 square units.

6.G-6#1.title: Cover the pool or fill it
6.G-6#1.text: Think about a swimming pool. In winter you pull a flat cover over the top. The size of the cover depends on the length and the width of the pool: that is area. In summer you fill the pool with water. How much water depends on the depth too: that is volume. One pool, two different questions, and two different kinds of unit.

6.G-6#2.title: One pair of numbers, three shapes
6.G-6#2.text: Use the numbers 6 and 4 three ways. A rectangle 6 by 4 has area 24. A triangle with base 6 and height 4 is half of that rectangle, so its area is 12. A prism with a 6-by-4 floor and a height of 2 stacks two layers of 24 cubes, so its volume is 48. Halve for a triangle. Multiply by a third number for a solid.

6.G-6#3.title: One room, three questions
6.G-6#3.text: A room is 5 long, 4 wide and 3 tall. "How much carpet covers the floor?" asks for area: 5 × 4 = 20 square units. "How much air is in the room?" asks for volume: 5 × 4 × 3 = 60 cubic units. "How much trim goes around the floor?" asks for perimeter: 5 + 4 + 5 + 4 = 18 units. The numbers are the same each time. Only the question tells you what to do with them.

6.G-6#4.title: Two squares side by side
6.G-6#4.text: An 8-by-4 rectangle is flat, so the question is about area. Cut it down the middle into two 4-by-4 squares. Each square covers 4 × 4 = 16. The two together cover 16 + 16 = 32 square units.

6.G-6#5.title: Whole box, then half
6.G-6#5.text: A triangle is flat, so this is area. Draw the rectangle around it, 6 wide and 9 tall. That rectangle covers 6 × 9 = 54. The triangle is half of it, and half of 54 is 27 square units. The half in the formula is this last step.

6.G-6#6.title: Make a ten first
6.G-6#6.text: Three edges mean volume, and the three numbers can be multiplied in any order. Pair 2 with 5 because they make 10. Then 10 × 3 = 30 cubic units. Looking for a pair that makes ten keeps the arithmetic short.

6.G-6#7.title: Double, then double again
6.G-6#7.text: A cube is a solid, so count cubes. The bottom layer is 4 by 4, which is 16 cubes. Two layers are 16 + 16 = 32. Four layers are double that: 32 + 32 = 64. The volume is 64 cubic units.

6.G-6#8.title: A parallelogram from two triangles
6.G-6#8.text: Flip a copy of the triangle and fit it against the first one. The pair makes a parallelogram with base 10 and height 3, covering 10 × 3 = 30. The triangle is one of the two equal parts, so its area is 30 ÷ 2 = 15 square units.

6.G-6#9.title: Count towers of cubes
6.G-6#9.text: "Inside" means filling the box, so count cubes. Look down on the 3-by-4 floor: it has 12 spots. On each spot a tower 2 cubes tall fits under the lid. Twelve towers of 2 make 24 cubes, so the space inside is 24 cubic units.

6.G-6#10.title: Cut and turn the tip
6.G-6#10.text: Use the leg of 5 as the base and the leg of 8 as the height. Cut the triangle straight across at half the height, 4 units up. Turn the small top triangle around and fit it beside the bottom piece. The result is a rectangle 5 wide and 4 tall, and 5 × 4 = 20 square units.

6.G-7#1.title: A plus sign
6.G-7#1.text: Take a plus sign in which every arm is 2 wide and 2 long. One way to slice it: five 2-by-2 squares, one in the middle and four arms, so 5 × 4 = 20. Another way: one long bar 6 by 2 across the middle, plus a 2-by-2 square above and one below, so 12 + 4 + 4 = 20. Different cuts, same simple pieces, same total.

6.G-7#2.title: Painting a wall
6.G-7#2.text: You paint the end wall of a house. The main part is 10 wide and 8 tall: 80. Above it is a triangular peak with base 10 and height 2. It is part of the wall, so add ½ × 10 × 2 = 10 to get 90. A window 3 by 2 is not painted, so take away 6. The paint covers 90 − 6 = 84 square units.

6.G-7#3.title: Two ways up the same wall
6.G-7#3.text: An L-shape is 7 tall on its left side. On the right side the same climb is made in two parts: a lower edge and an upper edge. If the lower edge is 3, the upper edge must be 7 − 3 = 4, because both routes go from the bottom to the top. The same works across: a bottom of 10 and a top piece of 4 leave a step of 6.

6.G-7#4.title: Count the columns by twos
6.G-7#4.text: Both rectangles are 2 tall, so every column of the joined shape holds 2 squares. The first rectangle has 3 columns and the second has 2, which makes 5 columns. Count by twos: 2, 4, 6, 8, 10. The total area is 10 square units.

6.G-7#5.title: Start from two equal pieces
6.G-7#5.text: Pretend both rectangles are 5 by 4. Two of them would cover 20 + 20 = 40. The second rectangle is really 5 by 3, which is one row of 5 squares smaller. Take that row away: 40 − 5 = 35 square units.

6.G-7#6.title: Two rectangles are left
6.G-7#6.text: With the square gone from a corner, cut the rest along a line level with the edge of the cutout. One piece is a full strip 6 wide and 5 − 2 = 3 tall, with area 18. The other is 6 − 2 = 4 wide and 2 tall, with area 8. The area left is 18 + 8 = 26 square units.

6.G-7#7.title: Level the roof
6.G-7#7.text: A triangle with base 8 and height 4 covers as much as a rectangle 8 wide and 2 tall. Swap the pointed roof for that flat block. The house becomes one rectangle 8 wide and 5 + 2 = 7 tall. Its area is 8 × 7 = 56 square units.

6.G-7#8.title: Split the leftover shape
6.G-7#8.text: Picture the 3-by-2 piece cut from a corner. Under the cut lies a full strip 10 wide and 6 − 2 = 4 tall, which covers 40. Beside the cut is a piece 10 − 3 = 7 wide and 2 tall, which covers 14. The area left is 40 + 14 = 54 square units.

6.G-7#9.title: Box the T, remove the corners
6.G-7#9.text: Draw a rectangle around the whole T: 9 wide and 6 tall, covering 54. The stem is only 3 wide, so beside it there are empty corners that are 9 − 3 = 6 wide in total and 4 tall. They cover 6 × 4 = 24. The T covers 54 − 24 = 30 square units.

6.G-7#10.title: Split into bar and stem
6.G-7#10.text: Take each corner to be 3 wide and 4 tall. The top bar is the full 10 wide and 8 − 4 = 4 tall, so it covers 40. The stem between the corners is 10 − 3 − 3 = 4 wide and 4 tall, so it covers 16. The T covers 40 + 16 = 56 square units.

6.G-8#1.title: Loading a moving truck
6.G-8#1.text: A truck is being packed with boxes that are all the same cube shape. Four boxes fit along the length of the floor and two fit across, so the floor holds 8 boxes. The boxes can be stacked 3 high. The truck holds 8 + 8 + 8 = 24 boxes, which is 4 × 2 × 3. If each box is 1 cubic foot, the truck space is 24 cubic feet.

6.G-8#2.title: Half of a half dollar
6.G-8#2.text: Think of money. Half of a dollar is 50 cents. Half of that half is 25 cents, a quarter of a dollar. So ½ × ½ = 1/4, and in decimals 0.5 × 0.5 = 0.25. The same thing happens with space: a cube that is ½ unit on each edge is so small that 2 × 2 × 2 = 8 of them fill one unit cube, so its volume is 1/8.

6.G-8#3.title: A table of cubes
6.G-8#3.text: Build cubes from small blocks and count. Edge 1: just 1 block. Edge 2: two layers of 4, so 8 blocks. Edge 3: three layers of 9, so 27 blocks, like a puzzle cube. Edge 4: four layers of 16, so 64 blocks. The list 1, 8, 27, 64 is what s³ gives for s = 1, 2, 3, 4.

6.G-8#4.title: It is a single layer
6.G-8#4.text: An edge of 1 means the box is only one cube thick. Lay it flat and it looks like a 3-by-5 rectangle of cubes. Count the rows: 5 + 5 + 5 = 15 cubes. With just one layer, the volume is the same number as the area of the floor: 15 cubic units.

6.G-8#5.title: Find the ten
6.G-8#5.text: The edges can be multiplied in any order. Pair 2 with 5 first, since 2 × 5 = 10. Then multiply by the edge that is left: 10 × 4 = 40 cubic units. This is like standing the box on its 2-by-5 face and stacking 4 layers of 10.

6.G-8#6.title: Row, square, cube
6.G-8#6.text: Build the cube in three stages. Put 3 blocks in a row. Lay 3 of those rows side by side to make a flat square of 9 blocks. Stack 3 of those squares to make the cube: 9, 18, 27 blocks. Each stage is 3 times the one before, which is what 3 × 3 × 3 means.

6.G-8#7.title: Two half cubes
6.G-8#7.text: The 1-by-2 floor is made of two unit squares. The box is only ½ tall, so above each square sits half of a unit cube. Two halves make one whole. The box holds exactly 1 cubic unit, even though one edge is 2 long.

6.G-8#8.title: Chop the stick and bundle it
6.G-8#8.text: This box is a long thin stick, ½ by ½ and 4 long. Chop it into four pieces that are each 1 long. Stand the four pieces together in a 2-by-2 bundle. The bundle is ½ + ½ = 1 wide, 1 deep and 1 tall. It is a unit cube, so the stick holds 1 cubic unit.

6.G-8#9.title: Halve the 8 first
6.G-8#9.text: Let the fraction meet the biggest even edge. Half of 8 is 4. Then multiply by the last edge: 4 × 3 = 12 cubic units. Halving 8 at the start keeps every number small, and the answer is the same 12.

6.G-8#10.title: Trap it between two boxes
6.G-8#10.text: The edge 3½ is halfway between 3 and 4. A box 3 × 2 × 4 holds 24 cubic units. A box 4 × 2 × 4 holds 32 cubic units. The real box must be halfway between them. Halfway between 24 and 32 is 28, so the volume is 28 cubic units.

6.G-9#1.title: Read it like a ruler
6.G-9#1.text: Lay a ruler along a horizontal segment. If one end sits at the 3 mark and the other end at the 11 mark, the segment is 11 − 3 = 8 long. You do not care where on the page the ruler lies. The points (3, 2) and (11, 2) work the same way: the shared 2 says where the ruler lies, and the x-values are the marks. The length is 8.

6.G-9#2.title: Read it like a thermometer
6.G-9#2.text: A thermometer is a vertical number line. If the reading climbs from 2 degrees to 9 degrees, it has risen 9 − 2 = 7 degrees. The points (4, 2) and (4, 9) are just like that. The shared x-value, 4, says which vertical line the thermometer stands on. The y-values are the two readings, and the segment is 7 units long.

6.G-9#3.title: From owing to having
6.G-9#3.text: Say you owe a friend 3 dollars, which is like standing at −3. Later you have 2 dollars of your own. How much money came in? You needed 3 dollars to pay off the debt and 2 more to keep, so 5 dollars. The amount is positive even though you started below zero. That is why the distance from −3 to 2 is 5.

6.G-9#4.title: Check by counting squares
6.G-9#4.text: A rectangle has corners (1, 2), (6, 2), (6, 5) and (1, 5). Across the bottom, x goes from 1 to 6, which is 5 units. Up the side, y goes from 2 to 5, which is 3 units. The area is 5 × 3 = 15. Draw it on a grid and count: 5 columns with 3 squares in each is 15 squares.

6.G-9#5.title: Hop along the line
6.G-9#5.text: Both points sit on the line y = 1. Start at x = 2 and hop one unit to the right each time. The hops land on 3, 4, 5, 6 and 7. That took 5 hops, so the segment is 5 units long.

6.G-9#6.title: Slide it down to the axis
6.G-9#6.text: Both points have x = 1, so the segment is vertical. Slide it down 2 units so the bottom end rests on the x-axis. The ends are now (1, 0) and (1, 4), and the length reads straight off: 4 units. Sliding moves a segment but does not stretch it.

6.G-9#7.title: Slide it to start at zero
6.G-9#7.text: Move the whole segment 3 units to the right. The point (−3, 4) lands on (0, 4) and the point (2, 4) lands on (5, 4). The length has not changed, and now it is easy to see: from 0 to 5 is 5 units. The negative sign is gone before any subtracting starts.

6.G-9#8.title: Two triangles from a diagonal
6.G-9#8.text: Draw the diagonal from (0, 0) to (4, 3). It cuts the rectangle into two right triangles, each with legs 4 and 3. Each triangle has area ½ × 4 × 3 = 6. The two together give 6 + 6 = 12 square units, the same as width times height.

6.G-9#9.title: Two rows of five
6.G-9#9.text: Sketch the rectangle on the grid. It is only 2 units tall, so it has 2 rows of squares. Each row runs from x = 0 to x = 5 and holds 5 squares. The area is 5 + 5 = 10 square units.

6.G-9#10.title: Split along the axes
6.G-9#10.text: The axes cut this rectangle into four pieces. Left of the y-axis the width is 2, and right of it the width is 3. Below the x-axis the height is 1, and above it the height is 2. The pieces are 2 × 1 = 2, 3 × 1 = 3, 2 × 2 = 4 and 3 × 2 = 6. Their sum is 2 + 3 + 4 + 6 = 15 square units.

6.G-9#11.title: Shift it off the negatives
6.G-9#11.text: Slide the rectangle 3 units to the right. Its left edge moves from x = −3 to x = 0, and its right edge moves from x = 4 to x = 7. A slide does not change the width. Now the width reads directly: from 0 to 7 is 7 units.

6.G-10#1.title: The hidden sides of a die
6.G-10#1.text: Hold a die and look at it from one corner. You can see at most three of its numbers. The other three are on the back and underneath. Now imagine the die unfolded into a flat cross of six squares. All the numbers from 1 to 6 show at once. A net does that for any box, which makes it easy to check that all six faces are counted.

6.G-10#2.title: Cardboard for a tissue box
6.G-10#2.text: A tissue box is 4 long, 2 wide and 3 tall. To make it you cut six pieces of cardboard. The top and bottom are 4 × 2 = 8 each. The front and back are 4 × 3 = 12 each. The two ends are 2 × 3 = 6 each. The cardboard needed is 8 + 8 + 12 + 12 + 6 + 6 = 52 square units, counting every face once.

6.G-10#3.title: A table of cube surfaces
6.G-10#3.text: Try a few edges and watch the pattern. Edge 1: each face is 1, so the surface is 6. Edge 2: each face is 4, so the surface is 24. Edge 4: each face is 16, so the surface is 96. Edge 10: each face is 100, so the surface is 600. Every time, you square the edge and then take 6 of them.

6.G-10#4.title: Label plus two lids
6.G-10#4.text: Think of a box as a label wrapped around four sides, with a lid on top and a lid on the bottom. For a box 4 by 3 on the floor and 2 tall, the label is 4 + 3 + 4 + 3 = 14 long and 2 tall, so it covers 28. Each lid is 4 × 3 = 12. The total is 28 + 12 + 12 = 52. The pairs formula gives 2 × (12 + 8 + 6) = 52 too.

6.G-10#5.title: Count the room you are in
6.G-10#5.text: A room is shaped like a rectangular prism. Look down: there is 1 floor. Look up: there is 1 ceiling. Turn all the way around and count the walls: 4. That is 1 + 1 + 4 = 6 flat surfaces. Every face has been looked at once, so the prism has 6 faces.

6.G-10#6.title: Strip around the sides
6.G-10#6.text: Unroll the four side faces into one strip. It is 3 + 3 + 3 + 3 = 12 long and 3 tall, so it covers 36. The top and the bottom are squares of 9 each. The total is 36 + 9 + 9 = 54 square units.

6.G-10#7.title: Sides first, then the ends
6.G-10#7.text: The four side faces make a strip 5 + 5 + 5 + 5 = 20 long and 5 tall. That strip covers 20 × 5 = 100. The top and bottom squares are 25 each, which adds 50. The surface area is 100 + 50 = 150 square units.

6.G-10#8.title: Wrap the 3-by-4 base
6.G-10#8.text: Stand the prism on its 3-by-4 face, so it is 2 tall. The distance around the base is 3 + 4 + 3 + 4 = 14. A strip that long and 2 tall covers the four sides: 14 × 2 = 28. The top and bottom are 12 each, adding 24. The surface area is 28 + 24 = 52 square units.

6.G-10#9.title: Write out all six
6.G-10#9.text: List every face instead of doubling at the end. Top and bottom: 2 and 2. Front and back: 3 and 3. Left and right: 6 and 6. Add them in order: 2 + 2 + 3 + 3 + 6 + 6 = 22 square units. Seeing six numbers in the sum is a quick check that no face was skipped.

6.G-10#10.title: Read the net as a strip
6.G-10#10.text: In the net, four rectangles sit in a row and fold around the 2-by-3 ends. That row is 2 + 3 + 2 + 3 = 10 long and 4 tall, so it covers 40. The two end flaps are 2 × 3 = 6 each. The whole net covers 40 + 6 + 6 = 52 square units.

6.G-10#11.title: A band and two big faces
6.G-10#11.text: Lay the prism on its 5-by-6 face, so it is 2 tall. A band around the four thin sides is 5 + 6 + 5 + 6 = 22 long and 2 tall, covering 44. The top and the bottom are 5 × 6 = 30 each, adding 60. The surface area is 44 + 60 = 104 square units.

6.SP-1#1.title: The balance point on a line
6.SP-1#1.text:
Mark the values 2, 3 and 10 on a number line and look for the spot where they balance. Try 5: the 2 is 3 below and the 3 is 2 below, a total of 5 below. The 10 is 5 above. The two sides match, so 5 is the mean.
Adding and dividing agrees: 15 ÷ 3 = 5.

6.SP-1#2.title: Line up by height
6.SP-1#2.text:
Five friends stand in a row from shortest to tallest. The third friend has two people on each side, so that friend's height is the median.
Now let them stand in any order. The person in the third spot could be the tallest of all, with nobody above. The middle spot only means something after the line-up is sorted.

6.SP-1#3.title: A class vote
6.SP-1#3.text:
A class votes for a pet: hamster, fish, hamster, lizard, hamster, fish. Hamster gets 3 votes, fish gets 2 and lizard gets 1, so the mode is hamster.
If one hamster vote changed to fish, both would have 3 votes and there would be two modes. If six students all picked different pets, nothing would repeat and there would be no mode.

6.SP-1#4.title: Level the stacks
6.SP-1#4.text:
Build three stacks of blocks with heights 4, 6 and 8. Take 2 blocks off the tallest stack and put them on the shortest. The 8 becomes 6 and the 4 becomes 6, so the stacks are now 6, 6, 6.
No blocks were added or lost, and every stack is level at 6. That level height is the mean.

6.SP-1#5.title: Think in tens
6.SP-1#5.text:
Each value is a number of tens: 1 ten, 2 tens and 3 tens. The mean of 1, 2 and 3 is easy to see, because 1 is one below 2 and 3 is one above, so they balance at 2.
The mean is 2 tens, which is 20. Scaling every value by 10 scales the mean by 10 as well.

6.SP-1#6.title: Count smaller and larger
6.SP-1#6.text:
Test each value without sorting. Is 3 the middle? Nothing is smaller than 3 and two values are larger, so no. Is 7 the middle? Two values are smaller and none is larger, so no.
Try 5: one value (3) is smaller and one value (7) is larger. The sides are equal, so the median is 5.

6.SP-1#7.title: Test each value by counting
6.SP-1#7.text:
A median of five values needs two values below it and two above. Test 8: the values 2, 5 and 4 are smaller, which is three, so 8 is too high. Test 4: only 2 is smaller, so 4 is too low.
Test 5: the values 2 and 4 are smaller, and 8 and 9 are larger. Two on each side, so the median is 5.

6.SP-1#8.title: Draw a quick dot plot
6.SP-1#8.text:
Put a dot above each value on a number line. The 2 gets one dot, the 4 gets two dots stacked up, and the 9 gets one dot.
The mode is the tallest stack. Only the stack above 4 is two dots high, so the mode is 4. The picture shows the answer with no arithmetic.

6.SP-1#9.title: Use the symmetry
6.SP-1#9.text:
Look at the list around 5. The 3 is 2 below and the 7 is 2 above, so they cancel and the mean is 5 without adding.
Cross off the two ends, 3 and 7. The pair 5, 5 is left, and halfway between them is 5, so the median is 5.
The only value that repeats is 5, so the mode is 5 too.

6.SP-1#10.title: Add, then divide
6.SP-1#10.text:
Check the balance answer with the usual recipe. The total is 4 + 6 + 8 = 18. There are three values, so share 18 into three equal parts: 18 ÷ 3 = 6.
As a second check, three values of 6 would also total 18. Both routes agree that the mean is 6.

6.SP-2#1.title: One score changes the average
6.SP-2#1.text:
Four quiz scores are 6, 7, 8 and 9. The total is 30, so the mean is 7.5. Now a teacher finds a marking mistake and raises the 6 to 10. The total grows by 4 to 34, and the mean grows to 8.5.
One changed score moved the mean by 4 ÷ 4 = 1 point. Every value has a share in the mean, so no value can change without the mean noticing.

6.SP-2#2.title: The new kid with 50 dollars
6.SP-2#2.text:
Five kids have 1, 2, 2, 2 and 3 dollars. The total is 10, so the mean is 2 dollars, which looks like everyone.
A sixth kid joins with 50 dollars. The total becomes 60 and the mean becomes 60 ÷ 6 = 10 dollars. Five of the six kids have 3 dollars or less, so a mean of 10 no longer describes a typical kid.

6.SP-2#3.title: Swap in something huge
6.SP-2#3.text:
Take 3, 5 and 8. The median is the middle value, 5. Change the 8 to 80 and the list is 3, 5, 80, with median 5. Change it to 8,000 and the median is still 5.
The means tell a different story: about 5.3, then about 29.3, then about 2,669. The big value still fills one seat at the end of the row, so the middle seat keeps the same value.

6.SP-2#4.title: House prices on one street
6.SP-2#4.text:
Five houses sold for 200, 210, 220, 230 and 900 thousand dollars. The total is 1,760, so the mean is 352 thousand. No house on the street sold for anything close to that.
The median is the middle price, 220 thousand, which sits right among four of the five houses. With one mansion in the data, the median gives the more honest picture.

6.SP-2#5.title: Pair off the ends
6.SP-2#5.text:
Match the smallest with the largest: 1 and 5 add to 6, so that pair averages 3. Match the next two: 2 and 4 also add to 6 and average 3. The value left over is 3 itself.
Everything balances at 3, so the mean is 3. It is also the middle of the list, which is why it feels typical.

6.SP-2#6.title: Start from the small values
6.SP-2#6.text:
The values 2, 3 and 4 have a mean of 3. Pretend the fourth value is 3 too, so the mean is still 3.
The real fourth value is 100, which is 97 more than 3. Share that extra among all four values: 97 ÷ 4 = 24.25. The mean climbs to 3 + 24.25 = 27.25, and nearly all of it comes from one number.

6.SP-2#7.title: Cross off the ends
6.SP-2#7.text:
Cross off the smallest value, 2, and the largest value, 100. Removing one from each end keeps the middle where it was.
The values 3 and 4 are left. The median is the point halfway between them, which is 3.5. The 100 was crossed off first, so its size never entered the answer.

6.SP-2#8.title: Count who is close
6.SP-2#8.text:
Estimate the mean: the total is close to 300, and 300 ÷ 4 = 75. Now ask how many salaries are within 10 of 75. None are, since the nearest ones are 35 and 200.
The middle two salaries are 32 and 35, so the median is halfway, 33.5. Three of the four salaries are within 4 of it. Report the median, 33.5.

6.SP-2#9.title: Cross off whatever is largest
6.SP-2#9.text:
Find the median of 4, 4, 10 by crossing off the smallest value and the largest value. One 4 and the 10 go, and 4 is left.
Now do the same with 4, 4, 1,000. One 4 and the 1,000 go, and 4 is left again. The largest value is removed whatever its size, so the median stays 4.

6.SP-2#10.title: Measure the gaps between neighbors
6.SP-2#10.text:
Put 2, 3, 4 and 100 on a number line and look at the spaces between neighbors. From 2 to 3 is 1. From 3 to 4 is 1. From 4 to 100 is 96.
Three values sit one step apart, and then there is an empty stretch of 96 before the last one. A value that far from every neighbor is an outlier, so yes, the 100 is an outlier.

6.SP-3#1.title: A week of temperatures
6.SP-3#1.text:
In one city the coldest day of the week was 12 degrees and the warmest was 30 degrees. The range is 30 − 12 = 18 degrees, so the weather swung a lot.
In another city the week went from 20 to 22 degrees, a range of only 2. If every day had been exactly 21 degrees, the range would be 21 − 21 = 0.

6.SP-3#2.title: Try it with eight numbers
6.SP-3#2.text:
Take 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 50. The bottom half is 1, 2, 3, 4, with middle 2.5. The top half is 5, 6, 7, 50, with middle 6.5. So the IQR is 6.5 − 2.5 = 4.
The range is 50 − 1 = 49 because of the 50. Change the 50 to 8 and the range drops to 7, but the IQR is still 4.

6.SP-3#3.title: Walk to the meeting spot
6.SP-3#3.text:
Four friends live at houses 1, 5, 6 and 8 on a street. They meet at the mean, house 5, because 20 ÷ 4 = 5.
Their walks are 4, 0, 1 and 3 houses long. A walk is never negative, whichever direction it goes. The total is 8, so the average walk is 8 ÷ 4 = 2 houses. That average walk is the MAD.

6.SP-3#4.title: Add the gaps
6.SP-3#4.text:
The list is in order, so measure the gap between each pair of neighbors. From 5 to 9 is 4. From 9 to 12 is 3. From 12 to 20 is 8.
The gaps join end to end and cover the whole stretch of the data: 4 + 3 + 8 = 15. That matches 20 − 5, so the range is 15.

6.SP-3#5.title: Sort, then count up
6.SP-3#5.text:
Write the list in order: 6, 9, 14, 22. Now the ends are the minimum and the maximum, with no scanning needed.
Count up from 6 to 22 in easy jumps. From 6 to 10 is 4, from 10 to 20 is 10, and from 20 to 22 is 2. The jumps total 4 + 10 + 2 = 16, so the range is 16.

6.SP-3#6.title: One stack on a dot plot
6.SP-3#6.text:
Draw the data as a dot plot. All three dots land in one stack above 3. The range is the width of the plot from the leftmost dot to the rightmost dot, and a single stack has no width.
A second check: the mean is 3, and each value is 0 away from it. Every measure of spread gives 0 here.

6.SP-3#7.title: Use the even spacing
6.SP-3#7.text:
The values 2, 4, 6 are evenly spaced, two apart. In an evenly spaced list of three, the middle value is the balance point, so the mean is 4.
On a number line, 6 is the very next value after 4, one step of 2 to the right. So the distance from 6 to the mean is 2.

6.SP-3#8.title: Two thirds of the values
6.SP-3#8.text:
Mark 2, 4 and 6 on a number line. The mean, 4, sits on the middle value. Two of the three values are 2 units away from it, and one is 0 units away.
So the average distance is two thirds of 2. Two thirds of 2 is 4 thirds, which is about 1.33. The MAD is about 1.33.

6.SP-3#9.title: Halfway between the ends
6.SP-3#9.text:
The values go up by 2 each time, so each half is evenly spaced, and the middle of an evenly spaced group is halfway between its ends.
Bottom half 1, 3, 5, 7: halfway between 1 and 7 is 4, so Q1 = 4. Top half 9, 11, 13, 15: halfway between 9 and 15 is 12, so Q3 = 12.
IQR = 12 − 4 = 8.

6.SP-3#10.title: List the values and add gaps
6.SP-3#10.text:
Write out what the dots say: 3, 3, 5, 8, 8. Now walk along the list and add up each move. From 3 to 3 is 0. From 3 to 5 is 2. From 5 to 8 is 3. From 8 to 8 is 0.
The moves total 2 + 3 = 5, the same as 8 − 3. The range is 5.

6.SP-4#1.title: Build one from quiz scores
6.SP-4#1.text:
Five quiz scores come in: 7, 8, 8, 9, 8. Draw a number line and add a dot for each score as you read it. One dot goes above 7, one above 9, and three pile up above 8.
The finished plot has five dots for five scores. The tall stack above 8 shows the most common score at a glance.

6.SP-4#2.title: Sorting ages into decades
6.SP-4#2.text:
At a family party the ages are 12, 15, 18, 21, 24, 27 and 29. Sort them by decade. The teens box gets 12, 15 and 18, so its bar is 3 tall. The twenties box gets 21, 24, 27 and 29, so its bar is 4 tall.
The two boxes meet at 20 with nothing between, so the bars touch. The bars alone no longer tell you that someone is exactly 24.

6.SP-4#3.title: Find the five numbers yourself
6.SP-4#3.text:
Take 2, 4, 4, 5, 7, 8, 10. The smallest is 2 and the largest is 10, so the whiskers end there. The middle value is 5, so the line inside the box goes at 5.
The bottom half 2, 4, 4 has middle 4, and the top half 7, 8, 10 has middle 8. The box runs from 4 to 8.

6.SP-4#4.title: Write the list behind the stack
6.SP-4#4.text:
Turn the stack back into numbers. Each dot above the 3 is one data value equal to 3, so the stack stands for the list 3, 3, 3, 3.
Count the entries in that list: there are four. So 4 values equal 3. Reading a stack as a list is a good way to check a count.

6.SP-4#5.title: Make a ten
6.SP-4#5.text:
Add the stacks in a friendlier order. The stack of 2 and the stack of 3 together hold 5 dots. The remaining stack also holds 5 dots. Two fives make 10.
You can check by writing the data out: 1, 1, 2, 2, 2, 2, 2, 3, 3, 3. That list has ten entries, so there are 10 values.

6.SP-4#6.title: Try it with real numbers
6.SP-4#6.text:
Use the data 10, 20, 30, 40, 50, 60, 70. The middle value is 40. The bottom half 10, 20, 30 has middle 20, and the top half 50, 60, 70 has middle 60.
So the box is drawn from 20 to 60 and the whiskers reach 10 and 70. The only summary number left is 40, and it is drawn inside the box. That line is the median.

6.SP-4#7.title: Compare with a bar graph
6.SP-4#7.text:
A bar graph of favorite pets has bars for cat, dog and fish. Those are separate things, and nothing lies between cat and dog, so the bars stand apart.
A histogram sits on a number line. After the range 0 to 9 the very next number is 10, which starts the next range. The line has no break, so the bars have no gap. Yes, they touch.

6.SP-4#8.title: Count up the grid lines
6.SP-4#8.text:
Go to the bar over 5–9 and climb it one grid line at a time, counting from the bottom: 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7. The top of the bar is at the seventh line.
Think of the bar as a stack of seven values, each somewhere from 5 to 9, such as 5, 6, 6, 7, 8, 9, 9. Seven values make a bar 7 tall.

6.SP-4#9.title: Ask each display a question
6.SP-4#9.text:
Ask both displays, "Where is the median?" On a bar graph of favorite foods there is nowhere to point. Pizza, tacos and pasta have no order, so they have no middle.
On a box plot you can point straight at the answer: the line inside the box. The edges of the box are the quartiles. The box plot is the one that shows them.

6.SP-4#10.title: Level the bars
6.SP-4#10.text:
Even out the bar heights without changing the total. Take 2 from the bar of 6 and give it to the bar of 2. The heights 4, 6, 2 become 4, 4, 4.
Three bars of height 4 hold 3 × 4 = 12 values. Moving counts between bars does not add or remove any, so the data set has 12 values.

6.SP-5#1.title: Describe it over the phone
6.SP-5#1.text:
Imagine telling a friend about a data set over the phone so they can sketch it. Say only "it is around 70" and they cannot draw anything yet. Add "the values go from 65 to 75" and they know how wide to make it. Add "most are in the middle, with the same amount on each side" and they can draw the hump.
Center, spread and shape are the three things the sketch needs.

6.SP-5#2.title: Try it with numbers
6.SP-5#2.text:
Look at 1, 1, 1, 2, 2, 3, 9. Six values crowd between 1 and 3, and the lone 9 trails far off to the right. This data is skewed right.
Flip it: 1, 7, 8, 8, 9, 9, 9 has its crowd on the right and a lone 1 trailing off to the left, so it is skewed left.
In 4, 5, 5, 6 both sides match, so it is symmetric.

6.SP-5#3.title: Ages at a birthday party
6.SP-5#3.text:
The ages at a birthday party are 9, 9, 10, 10, 10, 11 and 38. Six of the ages sit within two years of each other. That group is a cluster, and it tells you the party is for a ten-year-old.
The 38 is far from all of them. It is an outlier, and it has a story too: a parent is in the room.

6.SP-5#4.title: One number, three meanings
6.SP-5#4.text:
The number 80 means nothing until you know where it came from. A center of 80 points on a test says the class did well. A center of 80 minutes for a bus ride says the trip is far too long. A center of 80 degrees says to pack shorts.
The arithmetic is the same each time. The answer to the real question is different each time.

6.SP-5#5.title: Rule out the other names
6.SP-5#5.text:
Go through the words used for features of data. A cluster is a group of values close together, and the 30 is alone. A gap is an empty space, and the 30 is a value, not a space. The mode is the most common value, and 30 appears once.
The word for a single value far from the rest is outlier, so the 30 is an outlier.

6.SP-5#6.title: The fold test
6.SP-5#6.text:
Imagine folding the plot in half at the middle of the number line. If the two sides landed on top of each other, the data would be symmetric. Here they do not match: the left side is a tall pile and the right side is long and thin.
The side that sticks out long and thin is the tail. It is on the right, so the data is skewed right.

6.SP-5#7.title: Two buses, same typical time
6.SP-5#7.text:
Two bus routes both have a typical trip of 20 minutes. On the first route every trip takes between 19 and 21 minutes. On the second, trips take anywhere from 5 to 35 minutes.
You would plan your morning very differently for each one, yet the center is the same. The missing piece is how much the times vary, which is the spread.

6.SP-5#8.title: Sketch the dot plot
6.SP-5#8.text:
Draw the scores as dots: one dot above 7, three above 8, two above 9 and one above 10.
The tallest stack is at 8, so the center is 8. The dots run from 7 to 10, a width of 3 points. The stacks get shorter on both sides of the peak and no dot sits far away, so the shape is roughly symmetric.

6.SP-5#9.title: Set the 90 aside first
6.SP-5#9.text:
Cover the 90 and look at what is left: 20, 25, 25, 30. These balance at 25 and fit inside 10 minutes, so most students do about 25 minutes.
Now uncover the 90. It is 60 minutes beyond the next value, far outside that group, so it is an outlier. Report both facts: most about 25 minutes, one outlier at 90.

6.SP-5#10.title: Look at the gaps
6.SP-5#10.text:
Place the values on a number line. From 20 to 25 is 5, from 25 to 25 is 0, and from 25 to 30 is 5. Then from 30 to 90 is 60.
Four values crowd together on the left and one sits far away on the right. That long empty stretch ending in a single value is a tail pointing right, so the data is skewed right.

6.SP-6#1.title: A repeat still counts
6.SP-6#1.text:
Take the scores 7, 9, 9, 10. There are four scores, because the 9 was earned twice and both count. The total is 35, so the mean is 35 ÷ 4 = 8.75.
Someone who counts only the different numbers gets n = 3 and a mean of 35 ÷ 3, about 11.7. That is higher than every score, which cannot be right. One wrong count ruined the answer.

6.SP-6#2.title: Three centers, one data set
6.SP-6#2.text:
Try all three on 2, 3, 3, 4, 18. The total is 30, so the mean is 30 ÷ 5 = 6. The middle value of the sorted list is 3, so the median is 3. The value that repeats is 3, so the mode is 3.
Four of the five values are 4 or less. The median and mode match them, and the mean was pulled up by the 18.

6.SP-6#3.title: Same center, different scatter
6.SP-6#3.text:
The lists 9, 10, 11 and 1, 10, 19 both have a center of 10. A report that only says "center 10" makes them sound the same.
Subtract the smallest from the largest in each. The first gives 11 − 9 = 2 and the second gives 19 − 1 = 18. Now the report shows that one list hugs its center and the other is scattered wide.

6.SP-6#4.title: Use the skip-counting pattern
6.SP-6#4.text:
The values are the twos you say when skip counting: 2 × 1, 2 × 2, 2 × 3, 2 × 4, 2 × 5. The list stops at 2 × 5, so it has five values and n = 5.
That tells you the mean will divide by 5. Five is odd, so one value will sit alone in the middle, the third one.

6.SP-6#5.title: Pair them off
6.SP-6#5.text:
Circle the values two at a time: 11 with 13, then 15 with 17. That makes two pairs with nothing left over, so n = 2 × 2 = 4.
Nothing left over means the count is even. An even count has no single middle value, so the median will be found halfway between the two inside values, 13 and 15.

6.SP-6#6.title: Stack the dots
6.SP-6#6.text:
Draw a number line and place a dot for each value. One dot goes above 3. Two dots go above 5, one on top of the other. One dot goes above 7.
The mode is the tallest stack. The stack above 5 is the only one two dots high, so the mode is 5.

6.SP-6#7.title: Sort so repeats sit together
6.SP-6#7.text:
Rewrite the list in order: 2, 6, 6, 6, 9. Sorting pulls equal values next to each other, so repeats show up as a run.
The longest run is the three 6s in a row. The 2 and the 9 each stand alone. The value with the longest run is the mode, so the mode is 6.

6.SP-6#8.title: Balance around 5
6.SP-6#8.text:
Two of the four values are already 5, so guess that the mean is 5. Check the other two. The 3 is 2 below the guess and the 7 is 2 above it.
The 2 below and the 2 above cancel, so nothing pulls the balance point away from 5. The mean is 5, with no adding needed.

6.SP-6#9.title: Read it all off a dot plot
6.SP-6#9.text:
Draw the data: one dot above 3, two above 5, one above 7. Count the dots to get n = 4.
The picture is a mirror image around 5, with the tall stack in the middle, so the center is 5. The dots stretch from 3 to 7, and 7 − 3 = 4, so the range is 4. One sketch gives all three finds.

6.SP-6#10.title: Halfway between the ends
6.SP-6#10.text:
The values go up by 2 each time, so the list is evenly spaced and its middle is halfway between its two ends. Add the ends and halve: 2 + 10 = 12, and 12 ÷ 2 = 6.
Check by counting: 2 and 4 are below 6, and 8 and 10 are above it. Two on each side, so the median is 6.

6.SP-7#1.title: Ask five kids
6.SP-7#1.text:
Ask five sixth graders how tall they are and you might write down 142, 150, 147, 155 and 150 centimeters. No single one of those is "the" answer. To reply you would have to say something like "mostly around 150".
A question whose honest reply needs a list, and then a summary of the list, is a statistical question.

6.SP-7#2.title: One stack on the dot plot
6.SP-7#2.text:
Ask twenty people how many days are in a week. Every reply is 7. Plot the replies and you get one stack of twenty dots above 7, with a range of 7 − 7 = 0.
The twentieth reply told you nothing the first one did not. When the plot can only ever be one stack, the question is a fact question.

6.SP-7#3.title: Rewrite one question two ways
6.SP-7#3.text:
Start with "How long is my bus ride?" It is about one rider, and the reply is one number, such as 15 minutes.
Change the subject to a group: "How long are the bus rides of students at my school?" Now the replies might be 5, 15, 20 and 40 minutes. The topic stayed the same. Only the words naming who is being asked about changed.

6.SP-7#4.title: Picture the data you would get
6.SP-7#4.text:
Imagine collecting the data. You stand against a wall, someone marks your height, and you write down one number. A dot plot of this data has a single dot.
There is nothing to average, no smallest or largest, and no spread. A question that produces one dot is not statistical.

6.SP-7#5.title: Picture the dot plot
6.SP-7#5.text:
Imagine measuring everyone in the class and writing down numbers such as 140, 152, 147 and 160 centimeters. Plot them and the dots spread along the number line, some low, some high, with a few stacks.
To answer the question you would need to describe that spread-out picture. Data that spreads out comes from a statistical question.

6.SP-7#6.title: Check ten calendars
6.SP-7#6.text:
Look up February 2025 on ten different calendars. Each one shows 28 days. A list of the results is 28 written ten times, with no variation.
Compare "How many days are in each month of 2025?" That one gives 31, 28, 31, 30 and so on, which do vary. A number in the reply is not enough. The February question has one fixed reply, so it is not statistical.

6.SP-7#7.title: Time the lunch table
6.SP-7#7.text:
Imagine standing in the lunchroom with a stopwatch. One student is done in 8 minutes, another takes 15, and a slow eater takes 25. Your notebook fills with different times.
To report back you would say something like "most take about 15 minutes". Needing a summary of many different values is the sign of a statistical question.

6.SP-7#8.title: Wrong replies are not variability
6.SP-7#8.text:
Ask a hundred people and a few might say Los Angeles. Does that make the replies vary? No. Those people are mistaken, and a map settles it: the capital is Sacramento.
In a statistical question, different replies are all true at once, like different heights. Here only one reply is true, so the question is not statistical.

6.SP-7#9.title: Test the new question
6.SP-7#9.text:
Check the rewrite by imagining the replies. For "How many pets do I have?" you write one number, such as 2, and you are done.
For "How many pets does each family on my street have?" you knock on doors and write 0, 2, 1, 0, 3. Those replies differ from house to house. Adding the group turned one number into varying data, so the fix works.

6.SP-7#10.title: Look for the group word
6.SP-7#10.text:
Read the subject of the question: "sixth-graders". It is plural, so it points to many people, not one. You cannot look the reply up in one place or measure it once.
You would have to survey many students, and their sleep times would not all match. A group subject plus a quantity that differs between people makes the question statistical.

6.SP-8#1.title: Level three towers
6.SP-8#1.text:
Build towers of 2, 5 and 8 blocks. Take 3 blocks from the tallest tower and add them to the shortest. Now every tower is 5 blocks high.
No block was added or thrown away, so the 15 blocks are simply shared equally. The level height, 5, is the mean, and it matches 15 ÷ 3.

6.SP-8#2.title: The fourth runner home
6.SP-8#2.text:
Seven runners finish a race, and their times are written down in finishing order. The fourth runner has three people ahead and three behind, so that time is the median.
Suppose the last runner stops to tie a shoe and takes an extra hour. The fourth runner is still fourth, with the same time. The order had to be known first, and the slowest time did not matter.

6.SP-8#3.title: Four kids in a row
6.SP-8#3.text:
Four kids line up by height: 130, 134, 138 and 150 centimeters. No kid stands in the middle. But any height between 134 and 138 has two kids shorter and two kids taller.
To agree on one number, everyone uses the point halfway between the two inside kids. Add 134 and 138 to get 272, then halve it to get 136. No kid is 136 tall, and that is fine.

6.SP-8#4.title: Cross off from both ends
6.SP-8#4.text:
Cross off the smallest value and the largest value together: 3 and 11 go. Do it again with the new ends: 5 and 9 go.
Each round removes one value from each side, so the middle never shifts. The only value left is 7, so the median is 7.

6.SP-8#5.title: Find the point between
6.SP-8#5.text:
Put 2, 4, 6 and 8 on a number line. The median must have two values on each side, so it lies between 4 and 6.
The only whole number between them is 5. It is 1 step above 4 and 1 step below 6, so it is exactly halfway. Two values are below it and two are above. The median is 5.

6.SP-8#6.title: Step inward until you meet
6.SP-8#6.text:
The middle two values are 3 and 7. Put a finger on each and move both inward one step at a time. The fingers go to 4 and 6, and then both land on 5.
They moved the same distance, 2 steps each, so 5 is exactly halfway between 3 and 7. The median is 5.

6.SP-8#7.title: Move two blocks across
6.SP-8#7.text:
Picture stacks of 6, 8 and 10 blocks. Lift 2 blocks off the stack of 10 and set them on the stack of 6. All three stacks are now 8 high.
The total did not change, and the stacks are level, so each value's fair share is 8. The mean is 8.

6.SP-8#8.title: Share out the extra 95
6.SP-8#8.text:
Pretend for a moment that all four values are 5. The mean would be 5. The real last value is 100, which is 95 more.
Share that extra among the four values: 95 ÷ 4 = 23.75. The mean is 5 + 23.75 = 28.75.
For the median, cross off one 5 and the 100. The pair 5, 5 is left, so the median is 5. Report 5.

6.SP-8#9.title: Measure how far each center misses
6.SP-8#9.text:
See how close each center is to the actual values. The median, 5, is exactly equal to three of the four values.
The mean, 28.75, is 23.75 away from each 5 and 71.25 away from the 100. It is not close to a single value in the data.
The center that matches most of the data is the median, 5.

6.SP-8#10.title: Use the position formula
6.SP-8#10.text:
Count the values: n = 4. The middle position is (4 + 1) ÷ 2 = 2.5. There is no slot 2.5, so the median sits between slot 2 and slot 3.
Slot 2 holds 3 and slot 3 holds 7. Halfway between them is (3 + 7) ÷ 2 = 5. The median is 5, the same as crossing off gives.

6.SP-9#1.title: Rebuild the list from the plot
6.SP-9#1.text:
Suppose a plot has two dots above 4, one dot above 5, nothing above 6, and three dots above 7. Read it back into a list: 4, 4, 5, 7, 7, 7.
That is six values from six dots. The empty spot at 6 tells you no one got a 6. The plot and the list hold exactly the same information.

6.SP-9#2.title: Seven ages, two bars
6.SP-9#2.text:
Take the ages 12, 15, 18, 21, 24, 27, 29. Three of them fall in 10–19 and four fall in 20–29. The histogram is a bar of height 3 next to a bar of height 4.
Someone who sees only the bars knows that four people are in their twenties. They cannot tell whether anyone is exactly 24. The count is kept and the exact ages are dropped.

6.SP-9#3.title: Twelve students in a line
6.SP-9#3.text:
Line up 12 students from shortest to tallest and split the line into four groups of 3. The cut between groups 1 and 2 is Q1, the cut in the center is the median, and the cut between groups 3 and 4 is Q3.
The box covers groups 2 and 3. That is 6 of the 12 students, exactly half, whether their heights are close together or far apart.

6.SP-9#4.title: Make a tiny plot
6.SP-9#4.text:
Plot the data 5, 5, 6 yourself. Read the first 5 and draw a dot above 5. Read the second 5 and draw another dot on top. Read the 6 and draw a dot above 6.
Three values were read and three dots were drawn, one at a time. Each dot stands for one data value.

6.SP-9#5.title: Build the stack dot by dot
6.SP-9#5.text:
Work forwards from the measuring. Each time a measurement comes out as 3, one dot is added above the 3. After the first such measurement the stack is 1 high, then 2, then 3, then 4.
A stack 4 dots high can only come from four measurements equal to 3. So 4 measurements equal 3.

6.SP-9#6.title: Invent data that fits
6.SP-9#6.text:
Make up values that would create this bar, such as 10, 12, 15, 15 and 19. Each one lies in the interval 10–19, and each one raises the bar by 1.
Five values raise it to height 5. A sixth value in the interval would make the height 6, which is not what the bar shows. So 5 values fall there.

6.SP-9#7.title: Two lists, one bar
6.SP-9#7.text:
Here are two different data sets: 20, 20, 20, 20, 20, 20, 20, 20 and 21, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27, 28. Each has eight values between 20 and 29.
Both give the same bar of height 8 over 20–29. The bar tells you there are 8 values, but it cannot tell these two lists apart, so the exact positions are hidden.

6.SP-9#8.title: Count with eight values
6.SP-9#8.text:
Use the data 1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 7, 8. The bottom half 1, 2, 3, 4 has middle 2.5, so Q1 = 2.5. The top half 5, 6, 7, 8 has middle 6.5, so Q3 = 6.5.
The values inside the box, between 2.5 and 6.5, are 3, 4, 5 and 6. That is 4 of the 8 values, so the box holds the middle 50% of the data.

6.SP-9#9.title: Measure the four sections
6.SP-9#9.text:
Find the length of each piece. Left whisker: 6 − 4 = 2. Left part of the box: 7 − 6 = 1. Right part of the box: 9 − 7 = 2. Right whisker: 10 − 9 = 1.
The box is 1 + 2 = 3 wide and runs from 6 to 9, split at the typical score, 7. All four pieces together are 2 + 1 + 2 + 1 = 6, the range.

6.SP-9#10.title: Count up along the box
6.SP-9#10.text:
Start at the left edge of the box, 15, and count up to the right edge, 35. From 15 to 20 is 5. From 20 to 35 is 15. Together that is 5 + 15 = 20.
Add back to check: 15 + 20 = 35, which is the right edge. The box is 20 units wide, so the IQR is 20.

6.SP-10#1.title: Can a friend sketch it?
6.SP-10#1.text:
Read this summary: "Quiz scores are symmetric, centered at 8, and run from 6 to 10." A friend who never saw the scores can sketch a hump with its peak at 8 that fades out at 6 and 10.
Remove "centered at 8" and they do not know where the peak goes. Remove "from 6 to 10" and they do not know how wide to draw it.

6.SP-10#2.title: One sort, three answers
6.SP-10#2.text:
Take 9, 3, 6. Sort it once to get 3, 6, 9. Read the left end for the minimum, 3. Read the right end for the maximum, 9. Read the middle for the median, 6.
The range is 9 − 3 = 6. For the mean, add and share: 18 ÷ 3 = 6. A single sorted list gave everything except the sum.

6.SP-10#3.title: Five kids and their allowances
6.SP-10#3.text:
Five kids get weekly allowances of 5, 5, 6, 6 and 78 dollars. The total is 100, so the mean is 20 dollars. Four of the five kids get less than a third of that.
The median is the middle value, 6 dollars, which is what a typical kid here really gets. With the 78 in the data, the median is the center to report.

6.SP-10#4.title: Work in tens
6.SP-10#4.text:
Every value is a number of tens: 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 tens. The small list 1, 2, 3, 4, 5 adds to 15, and 15 ÷ 5 = 3.
So the mean is 3 tens, which is 30. Dividing every value by 10 first keeps the arithmetic small, and multiplying back by 10 at the end gives the same mean.

6.SP-10#5.title: Pair small with large
6.SP-10#5.text:
Match the smallest value with the largest: 2 + 8 = 10, so that pair averages 5. Match the two inside values: 4 + 6 = 10, so they average 5 too.
Both pairs balance at 5, so the mean of all four values is 5. This works because the values are evenly spaced.

6.SP-10#6.title: Count smaller and larger
6.SP-10#6.text:
Skip the sorting and test a value directly. The median of five values needs two values below it and two above.
Test 5: the smaller values are 3 and 1, and the larger values are 7 and 9. Two on each side, so the median is 5. Testing 7 fails, because three values (3, 1, 5) are smaller.

6.SP-10#7.title: Add up the gaps
6.SP-10#7.text:
Sort the list: 5, 7, 12, 18, 20. Measure the gap between each pair of neighbors: 2, then 5, then 6, then 2.
The gaps link the smallest value to the largest with nothing missed, so their sum is the range: 2 + 5 + 6 + 2 = 15. It agrees with 20 − 5.

6.SP-10#8.title: Count up from the minimum
6.SP-10#8.text:
The smallest value is 2 and the largest is 11. Start at 2 and count up to 11 in two jumps. From 2 to 10 is 8, and from 10 to 11 is 1 more.
The distance is 8 + 1 = 9. Check by adding back: 2 + 9 = 11, the maximum. The range is 9.

6.SP-10#9.title: Summarize from a dot plot
6.SP-10#9.text:
Draw one dot above each of 1, 3, 5, 7 and 9. Count five dots, so there are five values.
The dots are evenly spaced and the picture is a mirror image around 5, so the shape is symmetric and the center is 5. The leftmost dot is at 1 and the rightmost is at 9, and 9 − 1 = 8, so the range is 8.

6.SP-10#10.title: Pair the ends
6.SP-10#10.text:
Match the outside values: 10 + 50 = 60, and half of 60 is 30. Match the next two: 20 + 40 = 60, and half of 60 is 30. The value left in the center is 30.
Every pair averages 30 and so does the leftover value, so the mean is 30. Adding everything gives 150 ÷ 5 = 30 as well.

GEO-1#1.title: Everyday stand-ins
GEO-1#1.text: Use real objects as models. The tip of a sharp pencil pressed on paper marks a point. A string pulled tight between two nails is a segment, and you can measure it. A laser beam leaving a pointer is a ray: it has a start but no finish. A straight road imagined with no beginning and no end is a line, and a calm lake stretching forever in every direction is a plane. The real objects have thickness, but the ideas do not.

GEO-1#2.title: Read it off a ruler
GEO-1#2.text: Lay a ruler along the points so that A is at 0, B is at 12 and C is at 19. Each length is a subtraction of two ruler readings: AB = 12 − 0, BC = 19 − 12, AC = 19 − 0. When you add the first two, the reading at B is added once and taken away once, so it drops out and leaves AC. That only happens when B really sits between the other two readings.

GEO-1#3.title: Fold the number line
GEO-1#3.text: Mark −3 and 11 on a paper strip. Fold the strip so the two marks land on each other. The crease is the midpoint, and it falls at 4. Each mark travelled the same distance to the crease, 7 units, so the full gap is 7 + 7 = 14. That matches the formulas: 11 − (−3) = 14 for the distance and (−3 + 11) ÷ 2 = 4 for the midpoint.

GEO-1#4.title: Use ruler positions
GEO-1#4.text: Put A at the 0 mark of a ruler. B is 12 units along, so B sits at 12. C is 7 units past B, so C sits at 12 + 7 = 19. The length AC is the difference of the end readings, 19 − 0 = 19. Reading positions gives the same total as adding the two pieces, AC = 19.

GEO-1#5.title: Slide both points
GEO-1#5.text: Sliding two points the same amount does not change the gap between them. Move P and Q both 3 units to the right. P goes from −3 to 0 and Q goes from 9 to 12. Now one point sits at zero, so the distance is just the other coordinate. PQ = 12.

GEO-1#6.title: Count up from 18
GEO-1#6.text: Start at the 18 mark where B sits and count up to the end of the segment at 30. From 18 to 20 is 2. From 20 to 30 is 10. Together that is 2 + 10 = 12, so BC = 12. Counting up finds the missing piece without writing an equation.

GEO-1#7.title: Make a table of values
GEO-1#7.text:
Try values of x and watch the two halves.
x = 1: JM = 5, MK = 11. x = 2: JM = 10, MK = 14. x = 3: JM = 15, MK = 17. x = 4: JM = 20, MK = 20.
The gap shrinks by 2 each time, from 6 to 4 to 2 to 0. The halves match only at x = 4, where JM = MK = 20.

GEO-1#8.title: Step in from both ends
GEO-1#8.text: Put one finger on −3 and one on 11. Move both fingers one unit toward each other at the same time: −2 and 10, then −1 and 9, then 0 and 8, 1 and 7, 2 and 6, 3 and 5. On the seventh step both fingers land on 4. They moved equal distances, so 4 is halfway. Averaging agrees: (−3 + 11) ÷ 2 = 8 ÷ 2 = 4.

GEO-1#9.title: Count up in friendly jumps
GEO-1#9.text: Place X at 0 km, so Y is at 2.4 and Z is at 6.1. Count from Y up to Z in easy jumps. From 2.4 to 3 is 0.6. From 3 to 6 is 3. From 6 to 6.1 is 0.1. The jumps total 0.6 + 3 + 0.1 = 3.7, so YZ = 3.7 km.

GEO-2#1.title: Read angles on a clock
GEO-2#1.text: Look at the hands of a clock. They are two rays that meet at the centre, so the centre is the vertex. At 3:00 the hands make a square corner, a right angle of 90°. At 1:00 they are only 30° apart, which is acute. At 4:00 they are 120° apart, which is obtuse. If the hand tips are A and C and the centre is B, the angle is named ABC, with the centre letter in the middle.

GEO-2#2.title: Protractor readings subtract
GEO-2#2.text: Place a protractor at B with ray BA on the 0° mark. Suppose ray BD crosses at 25° and ray BC crosses at 73°. Then angle ABD is 25 − 0 = 25°, angle DBC is 73 − 25 = 48°, and angle ABC is 73 − 0 = 73°. Each angle is a difference of two readings, so adding the two small ones cancels the middle reading and leaves the big one: 25 + 48 = 73.

GEO-2#3.title: Try it with a sheet of paper
GEO-2#3.text: Take a sheet of paper. Draw a line from one corner into the sheet. It splits the square corner into two angles, perhaps 30° and 60°, and they add to 90° however you draw it. Those are complementary. Now pick a point on a straight edge and draw a line from it into the sheet. The two angles along the edge might be 110° and 70°. They always add to 180°, so they are supplementary.

GEO-2#4.title: Count up to 90
GEO-2#4.text: Start at 37 and count up to 90 in easy jumps. From 37 to 40 is 3. From 40 to 90 is 50. The jumps total 3 + 50 = 53, so the complement is 53°. This finds the missing angle by building up to the corner instead of subtracting.

GEO-2#5.title: Split off a right angle
GEO-2#5.text: A straight line is two right angles side by side. The 118° angle uses up one whole right angle and 28° of the second one, because 118 = 90 + 28. The other angle is what remains of the second right angle: 90 − 28 = 62°. Check: 118 + 62 = 180.

GEO-2#6.title: Use the full turn
GEO-2#6.text: The four angles at a crossing fill one full turn, 360°. The 65° angle and the one opposite it are equal, so together they use 65 + 65 = 130°. That leaves 360 − 130 = 230° for the other two angles. Those two are also opposite each other, so they are equal, and each is 230 ÷ 2 = 115°. The four angles are 65°, 115°, 65°, 115°.

GEO-2#7.title: Draw a bar for 90
GEO-2#7.text: Draw a bar that stands for 90°. One angle is two x-blocks. The other is one x-block plus a block of 30. Take the 30 block away from the bar: 90 − 30 = 60 is left, and it is made of three equal x-blocks. Each block is 60 ÷ 3 = 20, so x = 20. The angles are 2 × 20 = 40° and 20 + 30 = 50°.

GEO-2#8.title: Balance around 45
GEO-2#8.text: Two equal complements would be 45° each, because 45 + 45 = 90. The angle 37° is 8 below 45. To keep the total at 90, its partner must be 8 above 45, which is 45 + 8 = 53°. Check by adding: 37 + 53 = 90.

GEO-2#9.title: Use two quarter pizzas
GEO-2#9.text: The straight cut leaves a half pizza, which is two quarter pieces of 90° each. The 40° slice comes out of the first quarter and leaves 90 − 40 = 50° of it. The neighbour is that 50° piece plus the whole second quarter: 50 + 90 = 140°.

GEO-3#1.title: Turning off a straight road
GEO-3#1.text: Picture a straight road that crosses two parallel streets. To turn right onto the first street you swing the wheel through some angle, say 70°. At the second street you need exactly the same 70° turn, because that street points the same way as the first. If the two turns were different, the streets would point in different directions and would meet somewhere, so they would not be parallel.

GEO-3#2.title: Spin the Z half a turn
GEO-3#2.text: Mark the middle of the piece of transversal that lies between the two parallel lines. Spin the whole figure half a turn about that point. The transversal lands on itself, and each parallel line lands on the other one, because a half turn keeps a line pointing the same way. One corner of the Z lands exactly on the other corner. A turn does not change the size of an angle, so the two angles are equal.

GEO-3#3.title: Tilt a perpendicular
GEO-3#3.text: Start with a transversal that crosses both parallel lines at right angles. The two angles inside the C are 90° and 90°, which add to 180°. Now tilt the transversal by 15°. One inside angle closes to 75° and the other opens to 105°. Whatever one angle loses, the other gains, so the total stays at 180°.

GEO-3#4.title: Go through the C angles
GEO-3#4.text: Find the angle between the parallel lines that sits next to the 68° angle on the transversal. It is 180 − 68 = 112°. That angle and the wanted angle at the other crossing lie between the parallels on the same side, so they are co-interior and add to 180°. The wanted angle is 180 − 112 = 68°.

GEO-3#5.title: Share 180 in a ratio
GEO-3#5.text: The angles 3x and 2x are in the ratio 3 to 2, and together they make 180°. So the larger angle is 3 fifths of 180 and the smaller is 2 fifths. One fifth of 180 is 36. The angles are 3 × 36 = 108° and 2 × 36 = 72°, and one share is x = 36.

GEO-3#6.title: Watch the gap close
GEO-3#6.text: Try x = 10. The angles are 5(10) − 10 = 40 and 3(10) + 30 = 60, so the first is 20 behind. Each time x goes up by 1, the first angle gains 5 and the second gains 3, so the gap closes by 2. Closing a gap of 20 takes 10 more steps, which gives x = 20. Both angles are then 90°.

GEO-3#7.title: Use the full turn at one crossing
GEO-3#7.text: Look at one crossing. Its four angles make a full turn, 360°. The 47° angle and its vertical partner use 47 + 47 = 94°. The other two angles are equal to each other and share the remaining 360 − 94 = 266°, so each is 133°. The second crossing is a copy of the first because the lines are parallel, so the only sizes are 47° and 133°.

GEO-3#8.title: Slide the upper rung down
GEO-3#8.text: Imagine sliding the upper rung straight down the ladder until it lies on the lower rung. The rungs are parallel, so the rung does not turn as it slides. The 63° angle between ladder and rung rides down with it and lands exactly on the angle at the lower rung. A slide does not change an angle, so the lower angle is 63°.

GEO-3#9.title: One step with the C angles
GEO-3#9.text: Look between the two avenues on one side of the boulevard. The 55° angle at the first avenue and the obtuse angle at the second avenue are co-interior angles, the pair you trace with a C. Co-interior angles on parallel lines add to 180°, so the obtuse angle is 180 − 55 = 125° in one step.

GEO-4#1.title: A vending machine promise
GEO-4#1.text: Think of a vending machine: if you press button B4, then a juice drops out. Pressing B4 is the hypothesis and the juice is the conclusion. Many statements hide the same pattern. "All squares have four right angles" means "if a shape is a square, then it has four right angles." Rewriting it this way shows that being a square is p and having four right angles is q.

GEO-4#2.title: Dogs and animals
GEO-4#2.text: Start with a true statement: if it is a dog, then it is an animal. Converse: if it is an animal, then it is a dog. A cat shows that is false. Inverse: if it is not a dog, then it is not an animal. The same cat shows that is false. Contrapositive: if it is not an animal, then it is not a dog. That is true, because a rock that is not an animal cannot be a dog.

GEO-4#3.title: A pattern that finally breaks
GEO-4#3.text: Take the claim "n² + n + 41 is prime for every whole number n." Try n = 0, 1, 2, 3 and you get 41, 43, 47, 53, all prime. It keeps working up to n = 39. But n = 40 gives 1681, which is 41 × 41. Forty good cases proved nothing, and one bad case ended the claim. That is why a proof must give a reason for every step.

GEO-4#4.title: List the causes of wet ground
GEO-4#4.text: The converse says "if the ground is wet, then it is raining." List the ways ground gets wet: rain, a sprinkler, a hose, a spilled bucket, morning dew. Rain is only one item on the list. Seeing wet ground does not tell you which cause it was, so the converse is false, even though rain always gives wet ground.

GEO-4#5.title: Circles inside circles
GEO-4#5.text: Draw a circle for "angles that measure 90°" and a circle for "right angles." The statement says the first circle sits inside the second. Now pick anything outside the right-angle circle, such as an 89° angle. It must also be outside the 90° circle. In words: if an angle is not a right angle, then it does not measure 90°. That is the contrapositive, and the picture shows it is true.

GEO-4#6.title: Build one from two triangles
GEO-4#6.text: Take two equilateral triangles with side 1 and glue them together along one side. The outline has four sides and each has length 1, so the hypothesis holds. Its angles are 60° at two corners and 60 + 60 = 120° at the other two. A square needs four 90° angles, so this rhombus is not a square, and the claim is false.

GEO-4#7.title: Think of a mirror
GEO-4#7.text: The name gives it away: reflexive comes from reflect. A quantity looks in the mirror and sees itself, like 7 = 7 or AB = AB. The other properties need more than one thing. Symmetric turns AB = CD around into CD = AB, and Transitive links three quantities in a chain. In a figure, look for a side that belongs to two triangles at once. That shared side equals itself by the Reflexive Property.

GEO-4#8.title: Compare the requirement lists
GEO-4#8.text: Write what each shape needs. A rectangle needs four right angles. A square needs four right angles and four equal sides. The converse says that passing the short list guarantees the long list. It cannot, because the short list never mentions the side lengths. A door is a rectangle that is clearly not a square, so the converse is false.

GEO-4#9.title: Test it with coordinates
GEO-4#9.text: Put the points on a number line: A at 0, B at 3, C at 8 and D at 11. Then AB = 3 and CD = 3, so the Given holds. Now AC = 8 − 0 = 8 and BD = 11 − 3 = 8, so they are equal.
